remainingEvidence: The reachability conjunct is built and partly tested, so what remains here is narrower than construction: src/facets/runtime.ts#OperationContext declares a required `signal: AbortSignal`, and a Turn's cancellation reaches it through the scope signal TurnExecutor hands its executor, GatewayTurnInvocationPort's TurnGatewayScope, ComposedTurnGatewaySource.open calling operations(scope.signal), and the shared { signal, content } resources both DerivedDirectOperationContext and CanonicalBatchInvocationPort put on the handler's context. test/composition/mediation-pipeline.test.ts already discriminates the never-abort substitute over the concrete pipeline — 'the published mediation composition root runs each Operation under its own Turn's cancellation signal' asserts the handler's observed context signal is identically the Turn's signal and that an already-aborted Turn signal prevents dispatch with zero handler calls — but it carries no atom tag, so it is not yet conformance evidence for this row under scripts/quality/ledger.mjs's priority-evidence rule

What no test does is abort a Turn while an Operation handler is suspended and observe that handler's own context signal fire: the pipeline case aborts before invoke and then uses a controller it never aborts, and the only mid-execution abort observation in the suite is on a facet `start` hook's FacetLifecycleContext in test/operations/runtime.test.ts, not on an OperationContext. Availability at handler entry and observability during handler execution are different claims, and this rule makes the second one

The distinction this rule exists for is untested: an attempt whose wait the host abandoned must record `indeterminate` while an attempt whose handler observed its context cancellation must record `aborted` under C13-RECEIPT-FAILURE-KIND, and a mutation substituting a never-abort sentinel for the context signal must collapse the second case into the first rather than leaving both green

Propagation past the seam has no enforcement point at all. Nothing requires a handler that awaits further asynchronous work under its own invocation's lifetime to pass its context cancellation on, and nothing keeps a bound it derives linked to the cancellation it derived from. Closure needs a profile handler that delegates — §11.2 Shell is the sharpest, since P11-SHELL-CANCELLATION already asserts prompt cancellation — proving the abort reaches the side-effect owner, that awaited work reaches quiescence, and that a handler deriving a narrower deadline still aborts when the upstream cancellation fires

The schema exclusion is unchecked: OperationDescriptor.input accepts any JsonSchema, so nothing today refuses a declared input property that purports to carry cancellation, and nothing proves a handler cannot be reachable only through such a field. Verification requires the install-time manifest validation to refuse it, not the first invocation to fail on it

The durable-record boundary is satisfied by construction rather than by assertion, which is the direction a regression would come from: the ContentStore seam and the §8.5 command dispatcher take no signal, so an added one would silently widen this atom into the requirement it explicitly is not. A conformance assertion that those two seams stay cancellation-free is what keeps this rule from being read as requiring cancellation everywhere

Promotion to verified is blocked across a fragment boundary and the blocker is a true dependency rather than a bookkeeping accident: this row names C13-RECEIPT-FAILURE-KIND, which is W6's in invocations-audit.json and planned, so ledger.mjs's verified-status monotonicity rejects a verified row here until §7.4's failure-kind taxonomy is itself verified. remainingEvidence: The ordering half is built. FacetRuntimeHost resolves every BindingRequirement through FacetRequirementResolver in one pre-flight pass before the first start, so an unresolvable requirement is a rejected install raised before any Facet starts rather than a runtime failure or a degraded start, and the fail-closed default resolver admits only a Facet that declares no requirement.

Reliance is built and keyed on the exact provider FacetRef a dependent reached: a second installed Facet answering the same BindingName and a compatible FacetPackageId neither satisfies an unresolved requirement nor discharges an existing reliance. An edge lives from just before a dependent starts until its own stop has returned, so a provider stays resolvable for the whole of a dependent teardown its own withdrawal triggered, and reliance is independent of the child tree.

The withdrawal hold is built as a pending obligation rather than a rejection or a silent completion: FacetWithdrawal reports a `reliance` obligation, writes no plane while one stands, and retires the exact set once the last relying Facet goes inactive.

Pre-load rejection is built, and it is a W4 obligation this row may not cite: the Blueprint validator refuses a reliance cycle, named canonically from its lowest Facet id, and a requirement the validated platform compatibility does not admit. That evidence is carried by the W4 row C13-BLUEPRINT-VALIDATE-BEFORE-LOAD over src/definition/validator.ts and test/definition/validation.test.ts, and this row depends on it rather than restating it. Provider presence is deliberately NOT decided at validation: SPEC 9.1 forbids deriving a Package-closure obligation from a BindingRequirement, and the verified C13-PACKAGE-DEPENDENCY-DECLARED test validates a Blueprint whose manifest requires a Facet the closure does not install, so the liveness refusal belongs to the start gate above.

What remains is the §9.3 obligation shape itself, which is C13-BLUEPRINT-CONVERGENCE’s and W4’s: src/definition/reconciliation.ts#ReconciliationPlan carries opaque `blockers: readonly string[]` rather than a typed pending-obligation set, so a reliance hold cannot yet be carried by a reconciliation outcome. What the cut-point selector establishes now that every cut point has a runtime. The attribution half is evidenced as a join rather than as two facts side by side, which is the part a nearby test would miss: the last trace entry whose outcome is rewritten names alpha, and its after digest equals a digest recomputed over the persisted preparedArguments, so the record says this interceptor produced the value the PreparedInvocation froze. test/operations/runtime.test.ts#Facet runtime [C13-INTERCEPTOR-TURN-CONTEXT] refuses an operation selector at a Turn-bound cut point and keeps one at an operation cut point
remainingEvidence: Recorded discrimination, which is not this row's to write. Measured by hand in a detached worktree: deleting the isTurnBoundCutPoint conjunct from the InterceptorDeclaration constructor guard, and replacing isTurnBoundCutPoint's body with `return false`, each kill the cited selector from inside a cited symbol -- the fifteen-cell cut point x selector table then reports the three Turn-bound cut points admitting a narrowed selector. artifacts/quality/discrimination/facets.json is W0-owned and carries no attribution for a selector added after the last mutation run, so scripts/quality/discrimination.mjs would classify a verified row as DISC-STALE and fail the gate as a new addition; the row therefore stands at implemented rather than claiming a green it cannot yet evidence.

The claim's negative half is in the same test rather than a neighbouring one: the two operation cut points keep all three selectors, so the refusal is evidenced as a property of the cut point and not of the selector. A guard that refused every narrowed selector everywhere would pass a Turn-only assertion and fail this one.

test/operations/runtime.test.ts#Facet runtime [C13-INTERCEPTOR-TURN-HOSTED] returns a turn.step refusal as an attributed stop request and blocks the other Turn-bound cut points outright
remainingEvidence: Recorded discrimination, which is not this row's to write; the same W0-owned staleness that caps the sibling Turn-bound rows caps this one. Measured by hand in a detached worktree: collapsing orderSchedule's modeRank term kills the ordering selector from inside orderSchedule (the observed schedule becomes alpha/early/gate first), dropping its facetId comparison kills the same selector, restoring the unhosted-cut-point refusal in validateImplementations kills the admission selector from inside validateImplementations, and inverting the `cutPoint !== "turn.step"` test in TurnInterceptorRunner kills the stop-shape selector from inside TurnInterceptorRunner.

What the admission selector does and does not establish. It shows that a declaration at each Turn-bound cut point is admitted with its interceptor resolved, and -- in the same run -- that a declaration with no implementation behind it is still refused at each of them. So admission is the host executing these cut points rather than the correspondence check having stopped asking, which is the reading a bare admission assertion would leave open.

testSelectors: test/operations/runtime.test.ts#Facet runtime [C13-INTERCEPTOR-TURN-REWRITE] applies the cut point's rewrite rule to each rewriter's own answer rather than to the final value
remainingEvidence: Recorded discrimination, which is not this row's to write; W0 owns artifacts/quality/discrimination/operations.json and it carries no attribution for selectors newer than the last mutation run. Measured by hand in a detached worktree: moving the admit call after the loop so it sees only the final value kills the per-rewriter selector from inside TurnInterceptorRunner, and deleting the gate-fidelity comparison kills the mode-fidelity selector from inside the same symbol.

The per-rewriter selector is a join rather than two facts side by side: the refusal names the FIRST rewriter, and the recorded sequence of values offered to the rule is exactly one entry, so a runner that checked only the value it ended with would have admitted the illegal answer that the second rewriter overwrote. A test asserting only that the illegal answer was refused would pass against that defect.

This row's anchoring paragraph closes by restating rule 10 at the Turn-bound cut points -- a gate whose result differs from the value it received is refused here too -- and that clause is evidenced under C13-INTERCEPTOR-MODE-FIDELITY rather than here, by test/operations/runtime.test.ts#Facet runtime [C13-INTERCEPTOR-MODE-FIDELITY] polices a rewriting gate at every Turn-bound cut point instead of refusing the declaration it could not police. This row cited that test as a second selector and should not have: the label join is what proves a citation, and that test runs one interceptor per cell, so it can show gate fidelity and nothing per-rewriter. Adding this row's label to its title would have made the join claim the opposite. The clause is recorded here as cross-referenced, not as demonstrated by this row's own evidence.
